book: 026 - South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating

chapters.file: ch07 - How to Use this Book in a Philosophy Course.md
chapters.relation: Argues philosophy has a public-relations problem and that pop culture can fix it: just as Plato used the ring of Gyges and Descartes imagined a deceitful demon, The Matrix vividly pictures Cartesian deception and South Park's Cartman inheriting a million dollars dramatizes the problem of evil better than dry Jones-and-Brown cases. The chapter then advises instructors on using the chapters to introduce topics, assign summaries, and set reflection papers in intro courses, pointing to fan wikis and pop-philosophy.org so students need not be experts on the shows.

Introduces Part I by casting South Park, The Daily Show, and The Colbert Report as modern Socratic gadflies. It previews Young's comparison of the show's 'corruption of the youth' controversies to Socrates' trial, Arp's use of Johnnie Cochran's Chewbacca Defense to teach logic and fallacies, and Johnson's use of Colbert's 'wikiality' and 'truthiness' to attack relativism and the myth that everyone has a right to their opinion.

chapters.file: ch09 - The Talking Cure for Our Culture.md
chapters.relation: Young argues South Park is perceived as dangerous for the very reasons Socrates was executed — corrupting the youth and impiety — and that like Socrates it is really a gadfly promoting the examined life. Cartman is read through Arendt's Eichmann: evil as thoughtlessness, the inability to think from another's standpoint or ask if one can live with oneself, while Kyle and Stan's dialogues (such as deliberating Stan's grandfather's euthanasia request in 'Death') model the perspective-taking Arendt calls thinking. A final Freudian section explains the show's vulgarity as essential: jokes work like dreams, releasing repressed drives so the culture can talk through what it forbids.

Arp uses 'Chef Aid' — cartoon Johnnie Cochran's 'If Chewbacca lives on Endor, you must acquit' — to introduce the red herring fallacy, then teaches the basics of logic through South Park: Cartman's Tooth Fairy argument as deduction, Towelie's appearances as induction, and episodes like 'The Entity,' 'Weight Gain 4000,' and 'Butt Out' illustrating hasty generalization, slippery slope, false dilemma, appeal to inappropriate authority, and ad hominem. His point is that Parker and Stone deliberately violate logical principles for humor, and that spotting fallacies matters because bad reasoning drives laws, policies, and the beliefs people die for.

Johnson argues through Colbert's satire that truth is neither individual ('My Truth') nor cultural ('wikiality' — a Wikipedia entry does not become true by consensus), since relativism is self-contradictory and implies slavery was not wrong before abolition. He deploys Locke's attack on 'enthusiasm' to show 'truthiness' is circular reasoning — sure because one is sure — and dismantles the 'right to my opinion' as a bid to shield beliefs from evidence, closing with Socrates' model: when evidence runs out, admit ignorance and keep doing philosophy.

Frames Part II's epistemology chapters. Jacoby's chapter uses Stan Marsh debunking TV psychic John Edward, holistic healers, and Mormon belief to teach the ethics of belief against Pascal's wager; Lawrence's uses The Matrix to pose the skeptical problem and Descartes' response; Silverman's uses Adama's lie about Earth in Battlestar Galactica to raise the Gettier problem and the Clifford–James dispute over believing without sufficient evidence.

chapters.file: ch13 - Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress.md
chapters.relation: Jacoby reads Stan Marsh as W.K. Clifford's ethics of belief in action: from 'All About the Mormons' ('you better have something to back it up') to 'The Biggest Douche in the Universe,' Stan insists the burden of proof lies with claimants and that faith used as a fallback is no evidence at all. 'Cartmanland' and the story of Job serve to criticize Pascal's Wager — a good God would not eternally torment the virtuous nonbeliever, and the Wager simply assumes its afterlife payoff — while the harms of Miss Information's holistic healers, David Blaine's cult suicide, and Scientology show Clifford was right that comforting unsupported beliefs weaken minds and, as Stan tells John Edward, slow down the progress of all mankind.

Lawrence uses The Matrix to walk through Descartes' method of doubt: the dream argument, the evil demon reborn as a machine-run simulation, and invented worse cases ('Neo's Worst Nightmare,' a Matrix-within-the-Matrix that deceives even Morpheus' awakened rebels). The cogito is the only certainty that survives and Descartes' proof of God falls short, so certainty about the external world is unavailable; the chapter then borrows Russell's red-chair analysis of color, texture, and solidity to argue that even outside any Matrix, naive realism is false and we know only appearances.

chapters.file: ch15 - “You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”.md
chapters.relation: Silverman uses Adama's 'true lie' about Earth to motivate the Gettier problem: Starbuck's belief that Earth exists is true and justified by Adama's testimony, yet because that testimony is a lie, her justified true belief is not knowledge — just as Helo's true belief that the woman before him is 'Sharon' rests on mistaking Boomer for Athena. Goldman's reliabilism then questions whether sight, memory, and testimony are reliable belief-formers in a world of humanoid Cylons, weighing Hume's suspicion of testimony against Plantinga's defense of it. Finally Clifford's evidentialism is set against James's will to believe: the Colonials' forced, momentous choice to seek Earth shows that in an uncertain world pragmatic belief can be reasonable — 'so say we all.'

Frames Part III's metaphysics chapters. Lawrence's chapter uses The Matrix to survey dualism and the materialist theories of mind; Southworth's uses Wolverine's amnesia to test Locke's memory criterion and Jamie Madrox's duplicates for Parfit's view of identity; Pierce's asks whether Harry Potter's prophecies leave Harry free, probing compatibilism versus libertarian free will; and Littmann's asks whether Skynet's Terminators could be persons via a Terminator version of the Turing Test.

chapters.file: ch17 - The Role of Matter Biology or Function.md
chapters.relation: Lawrence asks which theory of mind best fits the Matrix trilogy. Cartesian dualism (with its pineal-gland plug standing in for Neo's headjack) would explain Neo's jackless mind in the Train Station but lacks evidence and faces the interaction problem, so the chapter defends a fully materialist reading — Neo's sentinel-destroying signal and burnt-eye sight reconstrued as Matrix hardware in his skull. It then contrasts reductive and eliminative materialism, Searle's beer-can biological naturalism, and functionalism via Lewis's Martian pain, concluding that the films' sentient machines — Agent Smith's seamless copy into Bane's body — presuppose functionalism.

Southworth tests Locke's memory theory on Wolverine: the Cassandra Nova/Xavier mind-swap shows identity follows mind, not body, and Wolverine's serial memory wipes (Team X, Weapon X, Apocalypse's brainwashing) mean that on Locke's connected-memory view several different people have inhabited his body — with House of M's total recall suddenly loading him with responsibility for all their deeds. Jamie Madrox's duplicates then carry Parfit's objection that shared memories cannot suffice for sameness of person, pushing toward physical continuity and the chapter's deflationary moral: be slow to judge who deserves blame.

chapters.file: ch19 - Time Travel and Fixed Time.md
chapters.relation: Pierce asks what kind of prophecies Trelawney's two 'real predictions' are, starting from Aristotle's problem of future contingents and Alexander of Aphrodisias on self-fulfilling prophecy: Dumbledore's point that Voldemort's choice marked Harry shows the prophecy did not cause its own fulfillment. The Prisoner of Azkaban time travel — later Harry had always cast that Patronus — plus special relativity support a fixed future on which Rowling's denial of destiny amounts only to libertarian openness, and the chapter concludes that the wildly improbable luck fulfilling the prophecies (Polyjuice in Moaning Myrtle's bathroom, the Sword of Gryffindor) makes best sense if some providential being is quietly guiding events.

chapters.file: ch20 - “Cyborgs Don’t Feel Pain. I Do.”.md
chapters.relation: Littmann asks whether Skynet's machines are people, testing three criteria on the Terminator films. The T-101 and T-1000 pass demanding Turing Tests by passing as humans; Searle's Chinese room — recast as a little Austrian inside the T-101 reciting 'Ahll be bahk' without understanding — shows behavior alone cannot prove thought; and feelings are equally unproven by behavior, since the T-101 can smile on command. But the films' first-person 'Terminator's-eye-view' sequences, Littmann argues, display what it is like to be a Terminator and thus prove machine consciousness, so humanity's extinction might not be the end of persons.

Frames Part IV's philosophy of religion chapters. Johnson's chapter sets Cartman's million-dollar theme park against God's goodness, with South Park characters giving answers echoing Calvin, Hick, and Job; Gallagher's uses Rose's 'I just know' on Lost and Aquinas' distinctions between knowledge, opinion, and faith to argue that faith is not knowledge; and Eberl and Vines' uses Battlestar Galactica's Cylon monotheism versus Colonial religion and atheism to ask whether God can be proven, whether evil disproves him, and whether life is meaningful without God.

chapters.file: ch22 - Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy.md
chapters.relation: Johnson turns 'Cartmanland' into a survey of answers to the problem of evil: Kyle's hemorrhoid-versus-Cartman's-wealth argument is the logical problem of moral evil; the story of Job fails because Job's continued belief does not rebut the evidence; Chef's 'sweet milk of our tears' mirrors Calvin's and Edwards' God-glorifying answer; and Stan's 'Cartman is totally miserable' restores Kyle's faith via second-order goods. The free will defense (via Augustine) handles moral evil but not natural evil, so the chapter closes with John Hick's soul-making theodicy — mirrored by South Park's Jesus saying life is about overcoming problems and growing — before conceding the evidential problem of evil still stands.

Gallagher reads Lost's Rose through Aquinas: faith is 'mid-way between knowledge and opinion,' sharing the certainty of episteme and the imperfection of doxa, so Rose's 'I just know' about Bernard's survival and her island cure confuses what she believes with what she knows. Aquinas' five ways ground natural knowledge that God exists, and the castaways' failures are diagnosed as sins against faith — Charlie's despair is acedia while Rose's certainty is the presumption (praesumptio) of elevating faith to demonstrated knowledge; the lesson is that faith perfects reason without replacing it.

chapters.file: ch24 - “You Have to Believe in Something”.md
chapters.relation: Eberl and Vines use Battlestar Galactica to weigh theism against atheism: Baltar's scientific rationalism meets Aquinas' five ways (the universe's ordered structure demands an unmoved, uncaused cause), Six's faith faces the problem of evil answered through Augustine on the perverse will and John Hick's soul-making (Starbuck's mother, 'your life is a testament to pain'), while Hume's faulty-architect analogy presses the atheist case. The chapter concludes with Russell's 'A Free Man's Worship': even in a Godless universe the Colonials find meaning in comradeship and humanity's survival — 'the gods shall lift those who lift each other.'

Frames Part V's ethics chapters. Adams' chapter updates Plato's ring of Gyges for Heroes — with Claire's and Sylar's powers, why be moral? — answered by the properly ordered tripartite soul; McAleer's uses The Office to illustrate Aristotle's wit as a mean between buffoonery and boorishness; White's uses the Batman/Joker problem and a Bat-trolley version of Foot's case to argue deontologically that Batman need not kill the Joker; and Loftis' reads Watchmen's Ozymandias and Rorschach as a failed utilitarian and a failed deontologist, pointing to 'who watches the watchmen.'

chapters.file: ch26 - But Isn’t It Only Natural.md
chapters.relation: Adams answers Plato's ring-of-Gyges challenge with Heroes: even when invisible, wrongdoing corrupts the wrongdoer, because justice is to the soul what health is to the body. Claire's refusal to claim credit for the fire rescue shows thumos (spirit) responsive to logistikos (reason), Sylar's uncontrollable hunger for powers is epithumetikon (appetite) ruling the soul, and Hiro's Vegas cheating shows how injustice makes life spin out of control; Claire's apology to Brody illustrates the Pagan Golden Rule — help your friends, harm your enemies — tempered by Plato's caution that enemies may become friends.

McAleer maps The Office onto Aristotle's ethics: David Brent is the buffoon who is 'the slave of his sense of humor,' Gareth the literalist boor who cannot take a joke, and Tim the ready wit whose irony responds to the situation — together illustrating that a virtue is a qualitative mean of acting and feeling appropriately, fixed by practical wisdom rather than rules. That humor cannot be codified mirrors the uncodifiability of Aristotelian ethics, and wit's very status as a virtue shows Aristotle's morality is broader than modern duty-and-outcome ethics: it aims at the flourishing (eudaimonia) of the whole person.

White asks why Batman never simply kills the Joker despite the graveyard he keeps filling, framing the question with Foot's and Thomson's trolley problem and the transplant-surgeon variant. Utilitarianism says kill one to save many; deontology says the agent-relative 'do not kill' — but the Batman case differs from the classic dilemmas because the Joker himself endangers his victims, Batman cannot be certain he will kill again (the foggy-track variant), and killing him would amount to the Minority Report-style prepunishment of a crime not yet committed. White, a self-described strict deontologist, concedes the case is genuinely hard and leaves the means-versus-ends debate open.

Loftis argues Watchmen's real target is authoritarianism, with Ozymandias and Rorschach as corrupted rationalizers. Ozymandias calls himself a consequentialist, but his Bentham-Mill utilitarianism cannot survive Dr. Manhattan's 'Nothing ever ends' — an infinite future makes utility sums impossible — and it ignores the rights of the New Yorkers he slaughters as mere means. Rorschach's deontology is hypocrisy (he admires Truman's Hiroshima trade-off and says 'can't make an omelet without breaking eggs'), mistaking Kant's categorical imperative — universalize your maxim, treat humanity never merely as a means — for black-and-white thinking in service of fascist thuggery, while the nonideological Nite Owls embody the lesson that no one should be trusted with such power.

holes.name: Sigmund Freud
holes.what: Founder of psychoanalysis: socially forbidden drives are repressed, and jokes — working like dreams — release repressed energy so it can be thought through (the talking cure).
holes.why: Chapter 9's closing section explains South Park's vulgarity as Freudian release — jokes break repression the way dreams do, the book's 'talking cure' for culture — and the taxonomy has no Freud entry.

holes.name: Informal Fallacies
holes.what: Named patterns of faulty reasoning — red herring, hasty generalization, slippery slope, false dilemma, appeal to inappropriate authority, ad hominem — in which the conclusion does not follow from the premises.
holes.why: Chapter 10 is an entire logic lesson built on South Park's Chewbacca Defense and other fallacy gags, and the taxonomy has no logic or fallacy concept at all.

holes.name: W.K. Clifford
holes.what: Victorian mathematician-philosopher who argued in 'The Ethics of Belief' that it is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone to believe anything upon insufficient evidence.
holes.why: Chapter 13's entire argument — Stan Marsh versus psychics, cults, and Pascal's Wager — is Clifford's ethics of belief, and chapter 15 relies on his evidentialism too.

holes.name: The Ethics of Belief (evidentialism)
holes.what: The doctrine that believing on insufficient evidence is morally wrong because beliefs guide action, harm others, and weaken the mind's powers of self-control and evidence-weighing.
holes.why: Chapters 13 and 15 both turn on evidentialism (against Pascal's Wager and for Clifford against James's will to believe), which no existing concept slug captures.

holes.name: Functionalism (philosophy of mind)
holes.what: The theory that mental states are functional input–process–output states realizable in any sufficiently organized system, biological or artificial.
holes.why: Chapter 17 argues functionalism is the theory of mind the Matrix films presuppose (sentient machines, Smith's seamless copy into Bane), against Searle's biological emergentism, and no taxonomy slug covers it.

holes.name: John Hick
holes.what: Twentieth-century philosopher of religion whose soul-making theodicy holds that God allows moral and natural evil so that free creatures can develop virtuous character through responding to it.
holes.why: Chapter 22's culminating answer to Cartmanland's problem of evil — echoed by South Park's Jesus and reused at length in chapter 24 — is Hick's soul-making theodicy.
